## <span id="page-35-0"></span>A Proofs

#### Proof of Proposition 1.

Preamble and part (i): Nash equilibrium. From eq. (6), we have

$$\pi_i = \Pi_0 + L \left[ \alpha_i \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_i^2 - \frac{\ell}{N} \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \right]$$

Differentiating with respect to  $\alpha_i$  (only the terms involving  $\alpha_i$  contribute, since the rivals' sum  $\sum_{j\neq i} \alpha_j$  is a constant from firm i's perspective):

<span id="page-35-1"></span>
$$\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i} = L \left[ \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - k \alpha_i \right]. \tag{13}$$

The second derivative is

$$\frac{\partial^2 \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i^2} = -kL < 0,$$

so  $\pi_i$  is strictly concave in  $\alpha_i$ .

Setting the first-order condition to zero:

$$L\left(s - \frac{\ell}{N} - k\alpha_i\right) = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \alpha_i^* = \frac{s - \ell/N}{k}.$$

Now,  $\alpha_i$  is restricted to the range [0, 1] (since it is the fraction of work automated).

If  $\alpha_i^* > 1$ , then since  $\frac{\partial^2 \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i^2} < 0$ ,  $\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i} > 0$  for  $\alpha_i < \alpha_i^*$ , so in this case, the maximum value of  $\pi_i(\alpha_i)$  occurs at  $\alpha_i = 1$ .

Similarly, if  $\alpha_i^* < 0$ , then  $\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i} < 0$  for  $\alpha_i > \alpha_i^*$ , so in this case, the maximum value of  $\pi_i(\alpha_i)$  occurs at  $\alpha_i = 0$ . Note that  $\alpha_i^* < 0$  if and only if  $s < \ell/N$ , i.e.,  $N < \ell/s = N^*$ ; this establishes the preamble claim that no firm automates when  $N \leq N^*$ .

Note that  $\alpha_i^*$  does not depend on any rival's choice  $\alpha_j$   $(j \neq i)$ : the rivals' automation levels enter only through the additive term  $-(\ell/N) \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j$ , which does not affect the first-order condition. Hence firm i's optimal strategy is independent of  $\alpha_{-i}$  (a dominant strategy), and is to set

$$\alpha_i = \frac{s - \ell/N}{k},$$

provided the right-hand side lies in [0,1]; otherwise  $\alpha_i = 0$  or  $\alpha_i = 1$  at the respective boundary. Since every firm solves the same problem, the unique symmetric Nash equilibrium has  $\alpha_i = \alpha^{NE}$  for all i. Part (ii): Cooperative optimum. Summing the per-firm profit (5) over all N firms, the sector's total profit is

$$\begin{split} \pi_{tot} &\coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{N} \pi_i \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ \Pi_0 + L \left( s \alpha_i - \ell \bar{\alpha} - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_i^2 \right) \right] \\ &= N \Pi_0 + L s \sum_i \alpha_i - L \ell N \bar{\alpha} - \frac{kL}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i^2. \end{split}$$

Using  $\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} = N\bar{\alpha}$ , this simplifies to

$$\pi_{tot} = N\Pi_0 + NL\bar{\alpha}(s-\ell) - \frac{kL}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i^2.$$

The first two terms depend on  $\alpha$  only through  $\bar{\alpha}$ ; the last term,  $-\frac{kL}{2}\sum_i\alpha_i^2$ , is maximized (least negative) when the  $\alpha_i$  are as equal as possible, by convexity of  $x^2$ . Formally, for any fixed  $\bar{\alpha}$ ,  $\sum_i\alpha_i^2 \geq N\bar{\alpha}^2$  with equality if and only if  $\alpha_i = \bar{\alpha}$  for all i (by the QM-AM inequality). Hence the optimum is symmetric:  $\alpha_i = \alpha$  for all i, and  $\bar{\alpha} = \alpha$ . Substituting:

<span id="page-36-0"></span>
$$\pi_{tot} = N\Pi_0 + NL\alpha(s - \ell) - \frac{kNL\alpha^2}{2}.$$
 (14)

This is a concave quadratic in  $\alpha$ :

$$\frac{\partial \pi_{tot}}{\partial \alpha} = NL(s - \ell) - kNL\alpha, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 \pi_{tot}}{\partial \alpha^2} = -kNL < 0.$$

Setting the first-order condition to zero:

$$NL(s-\ell) - kNL\alpha = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \alpha^* = \frac{s-\ell}{k}.$$

Since  $\pi_{tot}$  is strictly concave, this is the unique global maximum on  $\mathbb{R}$ . Restricting to  $\alpha \in [0,1]$ : if  $(s-\ell)/k > 1$ , strict concavity implies  $\partial \pi_{tot}/\partial \alpha > 0$  on [0,1], so the constrained maximum is  $\alpha = 1$ ; if  $(s-\ell)/k < 0$ , then  $\partial \pi_{tot}/\partial \alpha < 0$  on [0,1], so the constrained maximum is  $\alpha = 0$ . Thus

$$\alpha^{CO} = \frac{s - \ell}{k},$$

with boundary values 0 or 1 when the expression falls outside [0, 1].

Part (iii): Over-automation wedge. Suppose N > N<sup>∗</sup> , so α NE = (s − ℓ/N)/k > 0 by (i).

Case s > ℓ. Both (s − ℓ/N)/k > 0 and (s − ℓ)/k > 0, so neither rate is clamped at zero. Subtracting:

$$\alpha^{NE} - \alpha^{CO} = \frac{s - \ell/N}{k} - \frac{s - \ell}{k} = \frac{\ell - \ell/N}{k} = \frac{\ell (1 - 1/N)}{k}.$$

This is strictly positive for N ≥ 2 because ℓ > 0 and 1 − 1/N > 0.

For the comparative statics, write the wedge as W = ℓ(1 − 1/N)/k:

$$\begin{split} \frac{\partial W}{\partial N} &= \frac{\ell}{kN^2} > 0 & \text{(increasing in } N), \\ \frac{\partial W}{\partial \ell} &= \frac{1-1/N}{k} > 0 & \text{(increasing in } \ell), \\ \frac{\partial W}{\partial k} &= -\frac{\ell(1-1/N)}{k^2} < 0 & \text{(decreasing in } k). \end{split}$$

Part (iv): Boundary cases.

When s ≤ ℓ, then (s − ℓ)/k ≤ 0, so α CO = 0. So the wedge is α NE − α CO = α NE. Since we are in the setting where N > N<sup>∗</sup> , we have (s − ℓ/N)/k > 0. It is still possible, however, that (s − ℓ/N)/k > 1.

If s < k + ℓ/N, then α NE = (s − ℓ/N)/k, and this is the wedge. If s > k + ℓ/N, then α NE is a corner case, α NE = 1, and this is the wedge.

<span id="page-37-0"></span>Lemma 1 (Boundary cases). Write δ(µ) := µ ℓ λ(1−µ) for the additional planner correction beyond α CO. Then, for k > 0

- (i) α NE is interior if and only if ℓ/N < s < k+ℓ/N; Note that N > N<sup>∗</sup> is equivalent to s > ℓ/N.
- (ii) α CO is interior if and only if ℓ < s < k + ℓ;
- (iii) α SP (µ) is interior if and only if ℓ + δ(µ) < s < k + ℓ + δ(µ).

Each interval has width k. Because ℓ/N < ℓ < ℓ+δ(µ) for µ > 0, the three windows are progressively shifted to the right: interior automation arises at the lowest cost savings under Nash behavior, at intermediate savings under cooperation, and only at the highest savings under the social planner.

Proof of Lemma [1](#page-37-0). Each claim follows by checking when the raw formula lies strictly in (0, 1).

- (i) Nash equilibrium. From Proposition [1\(](#page-7-3)i), α NE = (s − ℓ/N)/k. The raw formula (s − ℓ/N)/k is strictly positive iff s > ℓ/N (i.e., when N > N<sup>∗</sup> ), and strictly less than one iff s < k + ℓ/N.
- (ii) Cooperative optimum. From Proposition [1](#page-7-3)[\(ii\),](#page-7-4) α CO = (s−ℓ)/k. The raw expression (s−ℓ)/k is strictly positive iff s > ℓ, and strictly less than one iff s < k + ℓ.

[^fig_2]

Figure 3: Interior regions for  $\alpha^{NE}$ ,  $\alpha^{CO}$ , and  $\alpha^{SP}(\mu)$  as functions of the cost saving s, where  $\delta = \mu \ell / [\lambda(1-\mu)]$ . Each shaded bar spans the values of s for which the corresponding automation rate is strictly interior. All three intervals have the same width k; they are shifted rightward by the progressively larger demand-loss terms that each objective internalizes.

(iii) Social planner. From Proposition 2(i),  $\alpha^{SP}(\mu) = (s-\ell)/k - \mu\ell/[\lambda(1-\mu)k]$ . Collecting terms,  $\alpha^{SP}(\mu) = (s-\ell-\delta(\mu))/k$ , which is strictly positive iff  $s > \ell + \delta(\mu)$  and strictly less than one iff  $s < k + \ell + \delta(\mu)$ .

Finally,  $\ell/N < \ell$  holds because  $N > N^* \ge 1$  (indeed  $N \ge 2$  in any strategic setting), and  $\ell < \ell + \delta(\mu)$  for  $\mu > 0$  since  $\delta(\mu) > 0$ .

**Proof of Corollary 1** (Frictionless limit, corollary of Proposition 1).

(i) With k = 0, firm i's profit from (6) becomes

$$\pi_i = \Pi_0 + L \left[ \alpha_i \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{\ell}{N} \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \right].$$

This is affine in  $\alpha_i$ , with slope  $L(s - \ell/N)$ . Crucially, the slope does not depend on rivals' choices  $\alpha_{-i}$  — rival automation affects the level of firm *i*'s profit (through the last term) but not the marginal return to  $\alpha_i$ . The optimal  $\alpha_i$  therefore does not depend on  $\alpha_{-i}$ , making it a dominant strategy.

When  $N > N^*$  (equivalently  $s > \ell/N$ ), the slope is strictly positive. Since  $\pi_i$  is linear and increasing in  $\alpha_i$  on [0, 1], the unique optimum is the upper boundary  $\alpha_i^* = 1$ . This holds for every firm simultaneously, so  $\alpha_i = 1$  for all i is the unique Nash equilibrium.

(ii) Assume additionally that the cost saving is less than the demand loss:  $s < \ell$ . With k = 0, aggregate profit from (5) is linear in  $\bar{\alpha}$ :  $\sum_i \pi_i = N\Pi_0 + NL(s - \ell)\bar{\alpha}$ . Since  $s - \ell < 0$ , this is strictly decreasing in  $\bar{\alpha}$ , so the profit-maximizing cooperative outcome is  $\bar{\alpha} = 0$  (no automation), yielding per-firm profit  $\Pi_0$ .

At the Nash equilibrium (α¯ = 1), per-firm profit is Π<sup>0</sup> + L(s − ℓ). Since s − ℓ < 0, we have Π<sup>0</sup> + L(s − ℓ) < Π0: every firm earns strictly less than under cooperation. The per-firm profit loss is Π<sup>0</sup> −[Π<sup>0</sup> +L(s−ℓ)] = L(ℓ−s). Across N firms, the total deadweight loss is NL(ℓ−s). For the demand loss, from eq. [\(2\)](#page-5-0):

$$D = A + \lambda w L N - \ell L N \,\bar{\alpha}.$$

At α¯ = 0: DCO = A + λwLN. At α¯ = 1: DNE = A + λwLN − ℓLN. Hence DCO − DNE = ℓLN.

#### Proof of Proposition [2](#page-10-0).

(i) The µ-planner chooses α¯ to maximize S(µ) = µ W + (1 − µ) K from [\(8\)](#page-10-1). We compute each derivative in turn. Recall that W = wLN[1 − (1 − η)¯α], so

<span id="page-39-1"></span>
$$\frac{dW}{d\bar{\alpha}} = -wNL(1-\eta). \tag{15}$$

Since ℓ = λ(1 − η)w, this equals −ℓ NL/λ. Recall that K = N[Π<sup>0</sup> + L((s − ℓ)¯α − k 2 α¯ 2 )] (e.g. eq. [\(14\)](#page-36-0)), so

<span id="page-39-2"></span>
$$\frac{d\mathcal{K}}{d\bar{\alpha}} = NL[(s-\ell) - k\bar{\alpha}]. \tag{16}$$

Combining:

$$\frac{dS}{d\bar{\alpha}} = \mu \, \frac{d\mathcal{W}}{d\bar{\alpha}} + (1 - \mu) \, \frac{d\mathcal{K}}{d\bar{\alpha}} = -\frac{\mu \, \ell \, NL}{\lambda} + (1 - \mu) \, NL \big[ (s - \ell) - k\bar{\alpha} \big].$$

Setting this to zero and dividing by NL > 0:

$$(1-\mu)[(s-\ell)-k\bar{\alpha}] = \frac{\mu\ell}{\lambda}.$$

Dividing both sides by (1 − µ) > 0 and isolating kα¯:

$$(s-\ell)-k\bar{\alpha} = \frac{\mu\,\ell}{\lambda(1-\mu)}, \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k\bar{\alpha} = (s-\ell) - \frac{\mu\,\ell}{\lambda(1-\mu)}.$$

Dividing by k, we find

<span id="page-39-0"></span>
$$\alpha^{SP}(\mu) = \frac{s - \ell}{k} - \frac{\mu \ell}{\lambda \cdot (1 - \mu) \cdot k} \tag{17}$$

This optimum will be valid as long as  $0 \le \alpha^{SP} \le 1$ . To find the bounds, define  $\bar{\mu}$  to be the value where  $\alpha^{SP}(\bar{\mu}) = 0$ . Then, solving for  $\bar{\mu}$ , we have

$$s - \ell = \frac{\bar{\mu}\ell}{\lambda \cdot (1 - \bar{\mu})}$$

$$\downarrow \downarrow$$

$$\bar{\mu} = \frac{\lambda(s - \ell)}{\ell + \lambda(s - \ell)}$$

From eq. (17), we have that  $\alpha^{SP}$  is decreasing in  $\mu$ , so if  $\mu > \bar{\mu}$ , then eq. (17) will be negative. Similarly, setting  $\mu$  to be the value where  $\alpha^{SP}(\mu) = 1$ , we have

$$s - \ell - k = \frac{\underline{\mu}\ell}{\lambda \cdot (1 - \underline{\mu})}$$

$$\psi$$

$$\underline{\mu} = \frac{\lambda(s - \ell - k)}{\ell + \lambda(s - \ell - k)}$$

Then for  $\mu \leq \underline{\mu}$ , we have eq. (17) is greater than 1.

#### (ii) Recall

$$S = \mu \cdot W + (1 - \mu) \cdot \mathcal{K} \qquad (\text{eq. (8)})$$

$$= \mu \cdot wLN \left[ 1 - (1 - \eta)\bar{\alpha} \right] + (1 - \mu) \cdot N \left[ \Pi_0 + L \left( (s - \ell)\bar{\alpha} - \frac{k}{2}\bar{\alpha}^2 \right) \right] \qquad (\text{eqs. (8) and (14)})$$

$$= N \left[ \mu wL \left( 1 - (1 - \eta)\bar{\alpha} \right) + (1 - \mu) \left( \Pi_0 + L \left( (s - \ell)\bar{\alpha} - \frac{k}{2}\bar{\alpha}^2 \right) \right) \right]$$

$$= \underbrace{N \left[ \mu wL + (1 - \mu)\Pi_0 \right]}_{a} + \underbrace{NL \left( -\mu \frac{\ell}{\lambda} + (1 - \mu)(s - \ell) \right)}_{b} \bar{\alpha} + \underbrace{\left( -\frac{(1 - \mu)NLk}{2} \right)}_{\frac{1}{2}\gamma} \bar{\alpha}^2$$

where in the linear term we used  $w(1-\eta)=\ell/\lambda$  from (3). This is a quadratic  $S=a+b\,\bar{\alpha}+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\,\bar{\alpha}^2$ , with  $\gamma=-(1-\mu)\,NLk<0$  strictly negative. Completing the square around the maximum  $x^*=-b/\gamma$ :

$$f(x) = a + bx + \frac{1}{2}\gamma x^2 = f(x^*) + \frac{1}{2}\gamma (x - x^*)^2$$

and therefore

$$f(x^*) - f(x) = -\frac{1}{2}\gamma (x - x^*)^2 = \frac{1}{2}|\gamma| (x - x^*)^2,$$

where the last equality uses  $\gamma \leq 0$ . Applying this with  $x^* = \alpha^{SP}(\mu)$ ,  $x = \alpha^{NE}$ , and  $|\gamma| = 0$ 

$$(1-\mu) NLk$$
: 
$$S(\alpha^{SP}) - S(\alpha^{NE}) = \frac{(1-\mu) NLk}{2} \left[\alpha^{NE} - \alpha^{SP}(\mu)\right]^2.$$

(iii) Recall from [\(9\)](#page-11-1), the wedge decomposes as:

$$\alpha^{NE} - \alpha^{SP}(\mu) = \frac{\ell(1 - 1/N)}{k} + \frac{\mu \ell}{\lambda(1 - \mu) k}.$$

The first term, ℓ(1 − 1/N)/k, is strictly positive because ℓ > 0 and N ≥ 2. The second term, µ ℓ/[λ(1 − µ) k], is strictly positive for any µ ∈ (0, 1) and equals zero at µ = 0. Hence α NE > αSP (µ) ≥ α CO for all µ ∈ [0, 1).

For worker income: from eq. [\(15\)](#page-39-1), W = wLN[1 − (1 − η)¯α] is affine and strictly decreasing in α¯ (since (1 − η) > 0 under the maintained assumption η < 1). Therefore α NE > αCO implies W(α NE) < W(α CO).

For owner surplus: from eq. [\(16\)](#page-39-2), dK/dα¯ = NL[(s − ℓ) − kα¯], which equals zero at α¯ = (s − ℓ)/k = α CO and is strictly negative for α > α ¯ CO (since k > 0). Hence K is strictly decreasing on (α CO, αNE], so K(α NE) < K(α CO).

Since both W and K are strictly lower at the Nash equilibrium than at the cooperative optimum, neither class can be made better off by moving from α CO to α NE: the Nash equilibrium is Pareto dominated.

Proof of Corollary [2](#page-13-1) (Sign of the externality). The wedge formula α NE − α CO = ℓ (1 − 1/N)/k is established in Proposition [1](#page-7-3)[\(iii\)](#page-7-1) for ℓ = λ(1 − η)w and s > ℓ. The three sign cases follow from the sign of ℓ: η < 1 gives ℓ > 0 (positive wedge), η = 1 gives ℓ = 0 (zero wedge, and both rates reduce to s/k), and η > 1 gives ℓ < 0 (negative wedge). At η = 0, ℓ = λw is maximal, so the wedge λw(1 − 1/N)/k is maximized. Note that η > 1 implies ℓ < 0 < s, so the interior condition s > ℓ holds automatically.

Proof of Proposition [3](#page-15-2) (Worker equity). With profit-sharing ϵ, aggregate demand satisfies

$$D = A + \lambda \left[ \underbrace{wLN(1 - (1 - \eta)\bar{\alpha})}_{\text{wage income}} + \epsilon \Pi \right],$$

where total profit is Π = D − P <sup>i</sup> C<sup>i</sup> = D − NL(w − sα¯ + k 2 α¯ 2 ). Substituting the expression for Π into the demand equation and collecting D terms on the left-hand side:

$$D(1 - \lambda \epsilon) = A + \lambda w L N(1 - (1 - \eta)\bar{\alpha}) - \lambda \epsilon N L \left( w - s\bar{\alpha} + \frac{k}{2}\bar{\alpha}^2 \right).$$

Expanding the right-hand side and grouping by powers of  $\bar{\alpha}$ :

$$D = \frac{A + \lambda(1 - \epsilon)wLN - \ell_{\epsilon}LN\bar{\alpha} - \lambda\epsilon\frac{k}{2}NL\bar{\alpha}^{2}}{1 - \lambda\epsilon},$$

where  $\ell_{\epsilon} := \ell - \lambda \epsilon s = \lambda (1 - \eta) w - \lambda \epsilon (w - c)$ .

(i) Cooperative optimum. The planner maximizes total profit  $\Pi = D - \sum_i C_i$  by choosing the common automation rate  $\alpha$  at a symmetric profile. Differentiating D (from the expression above) with respect to  $\alpha$ :

$$\frac{\partial D}{\partial \alpha} = \frac{-\ell_{\epsilon} LN - \lambda \epsilon kNL\alpha}{1 - \lambda \epsilon}.$$

Differentiating total cost  $\sum_{i} C_{i} = NL(w - s\alpha + \frac{k}{2}\alpha^{2})$ :

$$\frac{\partial(\sum_{i} C_{i})}{\partial \alpha} = NL(-s + k\alpha).$$

Setting  $\partial \Pi/\partial \alpha = \partial D/\partial \alpha - \partial (\sum_i C_i)/\partial \alpha = 0$  and rearranging:

$$NL(s - k\alpha) = \frac{\ell_{\epsilon}NL + \lambda \epsilon kNL\alpha}{1 - \lambda \epsilon}.$$

Multiplying both sides by  $(1 - \lambda \epsilon)$ :

$$(s - k\alpha)(1 - \lambda\epsilon) = \ell_{\epsilon} + \lambda \epsilon k\alpha$$

Expanding the left-hand side and collecting  $\alpha$  terms:

$$k\alpha \underbrace{\left[ (1 - \lambda \epsilon) + \lambda \epsilon \right]}_{-1} = s(1 - \lambda \epsilon) - \ell_{\epsilon}.$$

Substituting  $\ell_{\epsilon} = \ell - \lambda \epsilon s$ , the right-hand side becomes  $s - s\lambda \epsilon - \ell + \lambda \epsilon s = s - \ell$ . Hence  $k\alpha = s - \ell$ , giving  $\alpha^{CO}(\epsilon) = (s - \ell)/k$ , independent of  $\epsilon$ .

(ii) Nash equilibrium. Competitive pricing gives  $\operatorname{Rev}_i = D/N$ . The owner maximizes  $(1 - \epsilon)\pi_i$ ; since  $(1 - \epsilon) > 0$ , the FOC reduces to  $\partial \pi_i/\partial \alpha_i = 0$ . Since D depends on  $\alpha_i$  only through  $\bar{\alpha}$  (and the  $\bar{\alpha}^2$  term), and  $\partial \bar{\alpha}/\partial \alpha_i = 1/N$ , differentiating  $\operatorname{Rev}_i = D/N$  with respect to  $\alpha_i$  and evaluating at

a symmetric profile yields

$$\frac{\partial \operatorname{Rev}_i}{\partial \alpha_i} = \frac{1}{N} \cdot \frac{\partial D}{\partial \alpha_i} = \frac{-\ell_{\epsilon}L - \lambda \epsilon kL\alpha}{N(1 - \lambda \epsilon)}.$$

Combining with the cost derivative ∂Ci/∂α<sup>i</sup> = L(−s + kα), the symmetric FOC ∂ Rev<sup>i</sup> /∂α<sup>i</sup> − ∂Ci/∂α<sup>i</sup> = 0 becomes:

$$s - k\alpha - \frac{\ell_{\epsilon} + \lambda \epsilon k\alpha}{N(1 - \lambda \epsilon)} = 0.$$

Define N<sup>ϵ</sup> := N(1 − λϵ) + λϵ = N − λϵ(N − 1). Collecting the α terms on the left-hand side:

$$k\alpha \underbrace{\left[\frac{N(1-\lambda\epsilon)+\lambda\epsilon}{N(1-\lambda\epsilon)}\right]}_{=N_{\epsilon}/[N(1-\lambda\epsilon)]} = s - \frac{\ell_{\epsilon}}{N(1-\lambda\epsilon)}.$$

Multiplying both sides by N(1 − λϵ)/Nϵ:

$$k\alpha = \frac{s N(1 - \lambda \epsilon) - \ell_{\epsilon}}{N_{\epsilon}}.$$

Substituting ℓ<sup>ϵ</sup> = ℓ − λϵs into the numerator:

$$s N(1 - \lambda \epsilon) - (\ell - \lambda \epsilon s) = s [N(1 - \lambda \epsilon) + \lambda \epsilon] - \ell = s N_{\epsilon} - \ell.$$

Hence kα = (sN<sup>ϵ</sup> − ℓ)/N<sup>ϵ</sup> = s − ℓ/Nϵ, giving α NE(ϵ) = (s − ℓ/Nϵ)/k.

(iii) Wedge. Subtracting the cooperative optimum from the Nash rate:

$$\alpha^{NE}(\epsilon) - \alpha^{CO} = \frac{s - \ell/N_{\epsilon}}{k} - \frac{s - \ell}{k} = \frac{\ell - \ell/N_{\epsilon}}{k} = \frac{\ell(N_{\epsilon} - 1)}{k N_{\epsilon}}.$$

Since N<sup>ϵ</sup> = N − λϵ(N − 1), we have N<sup>ϵ</sup> − 1 = (N − 1) − λϵ(N − 1) = (N − 1)(1 − λϵ), so the wedge becomes

$$W(\epsilon) = \frac{\ell(N-1)(1-\lambda\epsilon)}{k N_{\epsilon}}.$$

To show the wedge is strictly decreasing in ϵ, write W = ℓ(N − 1)(1 − λϵ)/[k(N − λϵ(N − 1))] and apply the quotient rule. The numerator is f(ϵ) = 1 − λϵ with f ′ = −λ, and the denominator is g˜(ϵ) = N − λϵ(N − 1) with g˜ ′ = −λ(N − 1). By the quotient rule:

$$\frac{d}{d\epsilon} \left( \frac{f}{\tilde{g}} \right) = \frac{f'\tilde{g} - f\tilde{g}'}{\tilde{g}^2} = \frac{-\lambda[N - \lambda\epsilon(N-1)] + \lambda(N-1)(1 - \lambda\epsilon)}{N_\epsilon^2} = \frac{-\lambda}{N_\epsilon^2} < 0.$$

Hence ∂W/∂ϵ = −λℓ(N − 1)/(kN<sup>2</sup> ϵ ) < 0: the wedge is strictly decreasing. Setting W = 0 requires 1 − λϵ = 0, i.e., ϵ = 1/λ, which satisfies ϵ ≥ 1 whenever λ ≤ 1.

Proof of Corollary [3](#page-17-1) (Voluntary profit-sharing). Firm i chooses ϵ<sup>i</sup> ∈ [0, 1] to maximize retained profit (1 − ϵi)π<sup>i</sup> . Differentiating with respect to ϵ<sup>i</sup> :

$$\frac{d}{d\epsilon_i} [(1 - \epsilon_i)\pi_i] = -\pi_i + (1 - \epsilon_i) \frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \epsilon_i}.$$

When firm i shares ϵ<sup>i</sup> of its profit, its workers receive ϵiπ<sup>i</sup> and spend λϵiπ<sup>i</sup> in the sector. Firm i captures 1/N of the resulting demand increase, so ∂πi/∂ϵ<sup>i</sup> = λπi/N. Evaluating at ϵ<sup>i</sup> = 0:

$$-\pi_i + \frac{\lambda \pi_i}{N} = \pi_i \left(\frac{\lambda}{N} - 1\right) < 0,$$

since λ ≤ 1 and N ≥ 2. The derivative is negative at the left endpoint, so ϵ<sup>i</sup> = 0 is optimal regardless of the other firms' choices.

Proof of Proposition [4](#page-18-0). Partition the N firms into a coalition M of size M and a fringe of N −M non-members. Let

$$\alpha^F := \frac{1}{N - M} \cdot \sum_{i \notin \mathcal{M}} \alpha_i \tag{18}$$

be the average automation rate of fringe firms. At a symmetric profile where all coalition members choose αM, the average automation rate is

$$\bar{\alpha} = \frac{M\alpha^M + (N - M)\alpha^F}{N}.$$

From [\(6\)](#page-6-1), a coalition member i's profit is

$$\pi_i = \Pi_0 + L \left[ \alpha_i \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_i^2 - \frac{\ell}{N} \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \right].$$

Then

$$\pi_{i} = \Pi_{0} + L \left[ \alpha_{i} \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_{i}^{2} - \frac{\ell}{N} \left( \sum_{j \in \mathcal{M} \setminus \{i\}} \alpha_{j} + \sum_{j \notin \mathcal{M}} \alpha_{j} \right) \right]$$

$$= \Pi_{0} + L \left[ \alpha_{i} \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_{i}^{2} - \frac{\ell}{N} \left( \sum_{j \in \mathcal{M} \setminus \{i\}} \alpha_{j} + (N - M) \alpha^{F} \right) \right].$$

Under a symmetric strategy, where all firms in the coalition follow the same strategy α<sup>i</sup> = αM, we

have

$$\pi_{i} = \Pi_{0} + L \left[ \alpha^{M} \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \left( \alpha^{M} \right)^{2} - \frac{\ell}{N} \left( (M - 1) \alpha^{M} + (N - M) \alpha^{F} \right) \right]$$

$$= \Pi_{0} + L \left[ \alpha^{M} \left( s - \frac{\ell M}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \left( \alpha^{M} \right)^{2} + \frac{\ell}{N} (N - M) \alpha^{F} \right]$$

$$= \Pi_{0} + L \frac{\ell (N - M) \alpha^{F}}{N} + L \left[ \alpha^{M} \left( s - \frac{\ell M}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \left( \alpha^{M} \right)^{2} \right]$$

The coalition chooses α<sup>M</sup> to maximize P <sup>i</sup>∈M π<sup>i</sup> . At the symmetric equilibrium, P <sup>i</sup>∈M π<sup>i</sup> = Mπ<sup>i</sup> , so maximizing the individual firm's profit in the coalition also maximizes the coalition profits. Taking the derivative, we find

$$\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \alpha^M} = L \left( s - \frac{M\ell}{N} - k\alpha^M \right) = L \left( s - \frac{\ell}{N} - k\alpha^M - \frac{(M-1)\ell}{N} \right)$$

The additional term −(M − 1)ℓ/N (relative to eq. [\(13\)](#page-35-1)) arises because each coalition member internalizes the demand loss its automation imposes on the other M − 1 members, each of whom loses ℓL/N in revenue. Setting the first-order condition to zero:

$$\alpha^M = \frac{s - M\ell/N}{k},$$

clamped to [0, 1]. At M = 1, this reduces to α NE = (s − ℓ/N)/k. At M = N, it reduces to α CO = (s − ℓ)/k.

When both α<sup>M</sup> and α CO are interior, the residual wedge is

$$\alpha^M - \alpha^{CO} = \frac{s - M\ell/N}{k} - \frac{s - \ell}{k} = \frac{\ell(1 - M/N)}{k},$$

which is strictly positive for M < N and zero only at M = N.

Proof of Proposition [5](#page-19-1) (Pigouvian automation tax).

(i) Under the tax, firm i's profit from [\(6\)](#page-6-1) becomes

$$\pi_i = \Pi_0 + L \left[ \alpha_i \left( s - \tau - \frac{\ell}{N} \right) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_i^2 - \frac{\ell}{N} \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \right].$$

The first-order condition is s − τ − ℓ/N − kα<sup>i</sup> = 0, giving α NE(τ ) = (s − τ − ℓ/N)/k. Setting α NE(τ ) = α CO = (s − ℓ)/k yields τ <sup>∗</sup> = ℓ − ℓ/N = ℓ(1 − 1/N).

(ii) At τ = τ ∗ , all firms choose α CO. Per-firm profit is π tax = π(α CO)−τ <sup>∗</sup>LαCO = π CO −τ <sup>∗</sup>LαCO. Total tax revenue is τ <sup>∗</sup>LNαCO; rebated equally, each firm receives τ <sup>∗</sup>LαCO, restoring profit to π CO.

Proof of Proposition [6](#page-22-1) (AI productivity widens the over-automation wedge).

(i) At a symmetric profile α<sup>i</sup> = α with ϕ > 1, firm i's revenue is Rev<sup>i</sup> = DYi/(NY¯ ). The firm's first-order condition equates the marginal benefit of automation to its marginal cost: ∂ Rev<sup>i</sup> /∂αi+sL−kLα<sup>i</sup> = 0, where sL is the per-unit cost saving from replacing a worker with AI and kLα<sup>i</sup> is the marginal integration friction. Substituting the marginal revenue from [\(10\)](#page-22-0) and rearranging, the symmetric first-order condition is

$$k\alpha = s - \frac{\ell}{N} + \frac{D(\alpha)\left(\phi - 1\right)(N - 1)}{N^2[1 + (\phi - 1)\alpha]L}.$$

Define LHS(α) = kα and let RHS(α) denote the right-hand side. The left-hand side is strictly increasing (slope k). The right-hand side is strictly decreasing: the market-share term has numerator proportional to D(α) = A + λwLN − ℓLNα (decreasing in α) and denominator factor 1 + (ϕ − 1)α (increasing in α). Hence LHS = RHS has a unique solution. To show α NE(ϕ) > αNE(1), evaluate both sides at the baseline equilibrium α = α NE(1) = (s − ℓ/N)/k: LHS = s − ℓ/N, while RHS = s − ℓ/N + (positive market-share term) > LHS. Since LHS is increasing and RHS is decreasing, the unique crossing must occur at α NE(ϕ) > α NE(1).

(ii) The cooperative planner maximizes P i π<sup>i</sup> = D − P <sup>i</sup> C<sup>i</sup> . Total revenue equals aggregate demand D regardless of how output is allocated across firms: expenditure D is pinned down by [\(2\)](#page-5-0), so reallocating output shares does not change total revenue. The planner's first-order condition therefore depends only on costs:

$$\frac{\partial (\sum_{i} \pi_{i})}{\partial \alpha_{i}} = -\ell L + sL - kL\alpha_{i},$$

which is independent of ϕ. Setting to zero gives α CO(ϕ) = (s − ℓ)/k = α CO(1). For the generalized planner: S(µ) = µ W + (1−µ) K. Worker income W = wLN[1−(1−η)¯α] does not depend on ϕ. Owner surplus K = D− P <sup>i</sup> C<sup>i</sup> at symmetric profiles, and neither D [\(2\)](#page-5-0) nor C<sup>i</sup> [\(1\)](#page-5-2) depends on ϕ. Hence S(µ) is ϕ-invariant at every symmetric α¯, and α SP (µ; ϕ) = α SP (µ; 1) for all µ.

(iii) Combining (i) and (ii): α NE(ϕ) > αNE(1) while α SP (µ; ϕ) = α SP (µ; 1) for all µ, so the wedge α NE(ϕ) − α SP (µ; ϕ) is strictly larger than α NE(1) − α SP (µ; 1) for every µ. Since α NE(ϕ) is increasing in ϕ (by the same LHS/RHS argument with a larger market-share term), the wedge is strictly increasing in ϕ.

Proof of Proposition [7](#page-23-1) (Endogenous entry, frictionless benchmark). We assume k = 0 (frictionless case), λ = 1 (full recycling), 0 < κ < A (entry is costly but the market is viable for at least one firm), and ℓ > s (so that N<sup>∗</sup> > 1 by Corollary [1\)](#page-9-3).

Step 1: the profit schedule is strictly decreasing on N. Let m = ⌊N<sup>∗</sup> ⌋, so m ≤ N<sup>∗</sup> < m + 1. For N ≤ N<sup>∗</sup> , corollary [1](#page-9-3) gives α = 0, so by [\(5\)](#page-6-2) with λ = 1: Π<sup>∗</sup> (N) = A/N, which is strictly decreasing. For N > N<sup>∗</sup> , full automation is dominant (corollary [1\)](#page-9-3), and per-firm profit drops by ∆ = L(ℓ − s) > 0, giving Π<sup>∗</sup> (N) = A/N − ∆, also strictly decreasing. At the crossing: Π∗ (m) = A/m > A/(m + 1) > A/(m + 1) − ∆ = Π<sup>∗</sup> (m + 1). Hence Π<sup>∗</sup> is strictly decreasing on N.

Step 2: existence and uniqueness of NF E. Since κ < A, Π<sup>∗</sup> (1) = A > κ. Since ∆ > 0, Π∗ (N) → −∆ < 0 as N → ∞. The set S = {N ∈ N : Π<sup>∗</sup> (N) ≥ κ} is therefore nonempty and finite. Let NF E = max S. By strict monotonicity, Π<sup>∗</sup> (NF E) ≥ κ and Π<sup>∗</sup> (NF E + 1) < κ, so NF E satisfies [\(11\)](#page-23-2) and is unique.

Step 3: characterization by regime. We determine NF E by checking which integers are in S.

On the no-automation branch (N ≤ m): Π<sup>∗</sup> (N) = A/N ≥ κ iff N ≤ A/κ. So the viable integers on this branch are {1, . . . , min(⌊A/κ⌋, m)}.

On the full-automation branch (N ≥ m + 1): Π<sup>∗</sup> (N) = A/N − ∆ ≥ κ iff N ≤ A/(κ + ∆). The smallest integer on this branch is m + 1, so viable integers exist iff m + 1 ≤ A/(κ + ∆), i.e. κ + ∆ ≤ A/(m + 1). When nonempty, the viable set is {m + 1, . . . , ⌊A/(κ + ∆)⌋}.

Since NF E is the largest viable integer overall:

Case (i): (low entry cost) κ + ∆ ≤ A/(m + 1). The full-automation branch contains viable integers up to ⌊A/(κ + ∆)⌋ ≥ m + 1. Since κ + ∆ > κ, we have A/(κ + ∆) < A/κ, so the fullautomation branch's maximum does not exceed the no-automation branch's maximum in absolute terms, but it exceeds m (the cap on the no-automation branch). Hence NF E = ⌊A/(κ + ∆)⌋ ≥ m + 1 > N<sup>∗</sup> , and every firm fully automates. See fig. [4\(](#page-48-0)a).

Case (ii): (intermediate entry cost) κ + ∆ > A/(m + 1) and κ < A/m. The first condition means A/(m + 1) − ∆ < κ, so Π<sup>∗</sup> (m + 1) = A/(m + 1) − ∆ < κ. Since Π<sup>∗</sup> is decreasing, no integer above N<sup>∗</sup> is viable. The second condition gives A/κ > m, so ⌊A/κ⌋ ≥ m. Hence the largest viable integer on the no-automation branch is m, and NF E = m. Profit is Π<sup>∗</sup> (m) = A/m > κ (strict, since A/κ > m implies A/m > κ). In this case since NF E = m < N<sup>∗</sup> , no firm automates. See fig. [4\(](#page-48-0)b).

Case (iii): (high entry cost) κ ≥ A/m. Then A/κ ≤ m, so ⌊A/κ⌋ ≤ m. Since κ + ∆ > κ ≥ A/m > A/(m + 1), no integer on the full-automation branch is viable (same argument as case (ii)). Hence NF E = ⌊A/κ⌋. Since NF E = ⌊A/κ⌋ ≤ m ≤ N<sup>∗</sup> , no firm automates. See fig. [4\(](#page-48-0)c).

These three cases exhaust all κ ∈ (0, A). When κ > A, then NF E = 0.

[^fig_3]

<span id="page-48-0"></span>Figure 4: Per-firm profit as a function of the number of firms in the frictionless benchmark (k = 0, λ = 1). In each panel, profit follows A/N for N ≤ N<sup>∗</sup> (no automation) and drops discretely by ∆ = L(ℓ − s) at N<sup>∗</sup> when full automation becomes dominant. The red dot marks the free-entry equilibrium NF E. (a) Low entry cost: NF E lies above N<sup>∗</sup> and all firms automate. (b) Intermediate entry cost: NF E = ⌊N<sup>∗</sup> ⌋; the threat of automation deters the marginal entrant, sustaining positive profits without any automation occurring. (c) High entry cost: NF E falls well below N<sup>∗</sup> ; entry costs alone limit competition and the automation threshold is never approached.

Proof of Proposition [8](#page-24-2) (Endogenous entry with convex costs). First, we show that the per-firm profit is decreasing in N. From eq. [\(5\)](#page-6-2), we can write

$$\pi^{NE}(N) = A/N + C + g(N) \tag{19}$$

where

$$C := (\lambda - 1)wL \tag{20}$$

$$g(N) := L \alpha^{NE}(N) \left[ (s - \ell) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha^{NE}(N) \right]$$
 (21)

Since A/N is strictly decreasing on N, it suffices to show that g is weakly decreasing for N ∈ N. First, note that g(·) is decreasing in α NE

$$\frac{dg}{d\alpha^{NE}} = (s - \ell) - k \,\alpha^{NE} \tag{22}$$

By assumption ℓ > s, so the derivative is always negative. Then, by Proposition [1,](#page-7-3) we have

$$\alpha^{NE} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } N < \frac{\ell}{s} \\ \frac{s - \ell/N}{k} & \text{if } \frac{\ell}{s} \le N \le \frac{\ell}{s - k} \\ 1 & \text{if } \frac{\ell}{s - k} < N \end{cases}$$
 (23)

So α NE is non-decreasing in N. Thus g(α NE(N)) is non-increasing in N.

Since A/N is decreasing in N, and g α NE(N) is non-increasing in N, so π NE(N) = A/N + C + g(N) is strictly decreasing in N, i.e., π NE(N) > πNE(N + 1).

Now, let

$$S := \{ N \in \mathbb{N} : \pi^{NE}(N) \ge \kappa \} \tag{24}$$

Since π NE(1) = Π0(1) > κ by assumption, the set S is non-empty. To see that S is finite, we need to show that limN→∞ π NE < κ. First,

$$\alpha_{\infty} := \lim_{N \to \infty} \alpha^{NE}(N) = \min\left(1, \frac{s}{k}\right)$$
 (25)

So

$$\lim_{N \to \infty} g(N) = L \,\alpha_{\infty} \left[ (s - \ell) - \frac{k}{2} \alpha_{\infty} \right] < 0 \tag{26}$$

because s < ℓ (by assumption). Thus

$$\lim_{N \to \infty} \pi^{NE}(N) = \lim_{N \to \infty} [A/N + C + g(N)] = (\lambda - 1)wL + \lim_{N \to \infty} g(N) < 0$$
 (27)

Since C = (λ − 1)wL < 0. Since limN→∞ π NE < 0 < κ, the set S is finite. Let

$$N^{FE} := \max\left(N \in S\right) \tag{28}$$

Then π NE(NF E) ≥ κ and π NE(NF E + 1) < κ, so NF E satisfies [\(11\)](#page-23-2). If NF E > N<sup>∗</sup> , then α NE(NF E) = min (s − ℓ/NF E)/k, 1 > 0; since ℓ > s implies α CO = max{0, (s − ℓ)/k} = 0, we have α NE(NF E) > αCO, so over-automation persists.

Proof of Proposition [9](#page-26-1) (Endogenous wages). The symmetric equilibrium is a fixed point: α¯ such that α¯ = α NE(w(¯α)).

(i) At a symmetric rate α<sup>i</sup> = α for all i, we have α¯ = α and, from [\(5\)](#page-6-2),

$$\pi_i = \Pi_0 + L\left(s\alpha - \ell\alpha - \frac{k}{2}\alpha^2\right).$$

Aggregate profit is P i π<sup>i</sup> = N π<sup>i</sup> . Differentiating with respect to α and dividing by NL yields the planner's per-firm marginal benefit of automation:

$$g(\alpha) := s(\alpha) - \ell(\alpha) - k\alpha = w(\alpha) - c - \lambda(1 - \eta)w(\alpha) - k\alpha = w(\alpha) [1 - \lambda(1 - \eta)] - c - k\alpha,$$

where we used s = w − c and ℓ = λ(1 − η)w. By contrast, each firm's profit from [\(6\)](#page-6-1) depends on α¯ only through its own revenue share ℓ/N. Differentiating with respect to α<sup>i</sup> and dividing by L gives the private marginal benefit:

$$h(\alpha) \coloneqq s(\alpha) - \frac{\ell(\alpha)}{N} - k\alpha = w(\alpha) \left[ 1 - \frac{\lambda(1-\eta)}{N} \right] - c - k\alpha.$$

Differentiating, g ′ (α) = w ′ (α)[1 − λ(1 − η)] − k; the first term is weakly negative and k > 0, so g ′ < 0. The same argument applies to h (whose coefficient 1 − λ(1 − η)/N > 0 for N ≥ 2), so both are strictly decreasing. Note that g(α) = h(α) − ℓ(α)(1 − 1/N) for all α. At the NE fixed point, h(α NE) = 0 by definition, so

$$g(\alpha^{NE}) = 0 - \ell(\alpha^{NE})(1 - 1/N) = -\ell(\alpha^{NE})(1 - 1/N) < 0.$$

Since g is strictly decreasing and g(α CO) = 0 (the planner's optimality condition), the inequality g(α NE) < 0 = g(α CO) implies α CO < αNE.

(ii) From [\(7\)](#page-7-5), the threshold is N<sup>∗</sup> (w) = λ(1 − η)w/(w − c). Applying the quotient rule:

$$\frac{\partial N^*}{\partial w} = \frac{\lambda (1 - \eta)(w - c) - \lambda (1 - \eta)w}{(w - c)^2} = \frac{-\lambda (1 - \eta)c}{(w - c)^2} < 0,$$

so N<sup>∗</sup> is strictly decreasing in w. Since w ′ (¯α) ≤ 0 by assumption, w(¯α) ≤ w(0) for all α¯ ≥ 0. Combining: N<sup>∗</sup> (w(¯α)) ≥ N<sup>∗</sup> (w(0)), with strict inequality whenever w( ¯α) < w(0).

<span id="page-50-0"></span>Corollary 4 (Generalized planner under wage adjustment). Under the conditions of Proposition [9,](#page-26-1) let µ ∈ [0, 1) and define gµ(α) := s(w(α)) − ℓ(w(α))-1 + µ/(λ(1 − µ)) − kα. If g<sup>µ</sup> is strictly decreasing, then α NE > αSP (µ).

Proof sketch. The argument mirrors part (i) of Proposition [9,](#page-26-1) replacing the cooperative planner's marginal benefit g with the µ-planner's. The µ-planner maximizes S(µ) = µ W + (1 − µ) K over a common rate α, taking wages as given. From the proof of Proposition [2,](#page-10-0) the first-order condition is

$$(1 - \mu) [s(\alpha) - \ell(\alpha) - k\alpha] = \frac{\mu \ell(\alpha)}{\lambda},$$

which can be rewritten as gµ(α) = 0. This function relates to the private marginal benefit h(α) = s(α) − ℓ(α)/N − kα from the proof of Proposition [9](#page-26-1) by

$$g_{\mu}(\alpha) = h(\alpha) - \ell(\alpha) \left( 1 - \frac{1}{N} + \frac{\mu}{\lambda(1-\mu)} \right).$$

At the Nash equilibrium, h(α NE) = 0, so

$$g_{\mu}(\alpha^{NE}) = -\ell(\alpha^{NE}) \left(1 - \frac{1}{N} + \frac{\mu}{\lambda(1-\mu)}\right) < 0,$$

since ℓ > 0, N ≥ 2, and µ > 0. At the planner's fixed point, gµ(α SP (µ)) = 0 by definition. If g<sup>µ</sup> is strictly decreasing, the inequality gµ(α NE) < 0 = gµ(α SP ) implies α SP (µ) < αNE, exactly as in the µ = 0 case.

It remains to verify monotonicity. Differentiating:

$$g'_{\mu}(\alpha) = w'(\alpha) \left[ 1 - (1 - \eta) \left( \lambda + \frac{\mu}{1 - \mu} \right) \right] - k.$$

Define the bracket as C<sup>µ</sup> := 1 − (1 − η)[λ + µ/(1 − µ)]. At µ = 0, C<sup>0</sup> = 1 − λ(1 − η) ≥ 0, which is the coefficient used in the proof of Proposition [9;](#page-26-1) since w ′ ≤ 0, the product w ′C<sup>0</sup> ≤ 0 and g ′ <sup>0</sup> < 0 follows immediately. For µ > 0, C<sup>µ</sup> decreases. As long as C<sup>µ</sup> ≥ 0, the same argument applies; this holds for all µ ≤ µ¯ := [1 − (1 − η)λ]/[2 − η − (1 − η)λ] (approximately 0.48 at λ = 0.5, η = 0.30). When C<sup>µ</sup> < 0, the product w ′C<sup>µ</sup> ≥ 0, so g ′ <sup>µ</sup> < 0 requires k > |w ′ (α)| · |Cµ|: integration frictions must dominate wage sensitivity.

As a numerical illustration, consider w( ¯α) = 1 − 0.5 ¯α, c = 0.30, λ = 0.5, η = 0.30, k = 1, N = 7, and µ = 0.3. The equilibrium rates are α NE ≈ 0.44, α CO ≈ 0.26, and α SP (0.3) ≈ 0.04, confirming α SP < αCO < αNE. The distributional premium is substantial: the µ-planner would reduce automation to near zero, well below the cooperative optimum that already lies far below the Nash rate.

Proof of Proposition [10](#page-27-1) (Capital income recycling). We derive the result for general k ≥ 0; the proposition's two parts follow from the k = 0 specialization.

Aggregate demand is D = A + λwLN − ℓLNα¯ + ˆηΠ, where total profit is Π = D − NL(w − sα¯) − k 2 L P j α 2 j . Substituting and solving for D:

$$D(1-\hat{\eta}) = A + (\lambda - \hat{\eta})wLN - \ell_{\hat{\eta}} LN\bar{\alpha} - \frac{\hat{\eta}k}{2}L\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}^{2},$$

with ℓη<sup>ˆ</sup> = ℓ − ηsˆ . When k = 0 this gives [\(12\)](#page-27-0). Since Nα¯ = α<sup>i</sup> + P <sup>j</sup≯=<sup>i</sup> α<sup>j</sup> , differentiating:

$$\frac{\partial D}{\partial \alpha_i} = -\frac{\ell_{\hat{\eta}} L}{1 - \hat{\eta}} - \frac{\hat{\eta} k L}{1 - \hat{\eta}} \alpha_i.$$

Revenue Rev<sup>i</sup> = D/N gives ∂ Rev<sup>i</sup> /∂α<sup>i</sup> = −ℓηˆL/[N(1 − ηˆ)] − ηkLα ˆ <sup>i</sup>/[N(1 − ηˆ)]. Firm i's marginal profit, including the direct cost saving sL and marginal friction kLα<sup>i</sup> , is

$$\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial \alpha_i} = L \left( s - \frac{\ell_{\hat{\eta}}}{N(1 - \hat{\eta})} - k\alpha_i \cdot \frac{\hat{N}}{N(1 - \hat{\eta})} \right),$$

where Nˆ := N(1 − ηˆ) + ˆη. This depends only on α<sup>i</sup> , so the equilibrium is in strictly dominant strategies.

Part (i): k = 0. The marginal profit reduces to L(s − ℓηˆ/[N(1 − ηˆ)]), a constant independent of α<sup>i</sup> . This is positive if and only if sN(1 <sup>−</sup> <sup>η</sup>ˆ) > ℓηˆ, i.e. N > <sup>ℓ</sup>η<sup>ˆ</sup> <sup>s</sup>(1−ηˆ) = Nηˆ. Thus full automation is strictly dominant when N > Nη<sup>ˆ</sup> and no automation is strictly dominant when N < Nηˆ, reproducing the structure of Corollary [1.](#page-9-3)

Part (ii). ℓη<sup>ˆ</sup> = ℓ − ηsˆ ≤ 0 if and only if ηˆ ≥ ℓ/s.

Extension to k > 0. Setting the first-order condition to zero:

$$\alpha^{NE} = \frac{N(1-\hat{\eta})}{k\hat{N}} \left( s - \frac{\ell_{\hat{\eta}}}{N(1-\hat{\eta})} \right) = \frac{s\hat{N} - \ell}{k\hat{N}} = \frac{s - \ell/\hat{N}}{k}.$$

This is positive if and only if N > N ˆ <sup>∗</sup> , reproducing Proposition [1](#page-7-3) with N replaced by Nˆ. At a symmetric profile (α<sup>j</sup> = α for all j), total profit is Π = <sup>N</sup> 1−ηˆ [Π<sup>0</sup> + L(s − ℓ)α − k 2 Lα<sup>2</sup> ]. The 1/(1 − ηˆ) multiplier scales the objective without changing the optimizer, so α CO = max{0, (s − ℓ)/k}, the same as in Proposition [1.](#page-7-3)
